name: Candle Cove
description: A short horror fiction piece by webcomic author Kris Straub, published in 2009 on the Ichor Falls website. Written in the form of a forum thread in which adults remember a disturbing 1970s children's television program called 'Candle Cove' that turns out never to have existed.
full_description: Candle Cove is a creepypasta short story written by American webcomic author Kris Straub and published on his fiction site Ichor Falls in 2009. The piece is presented as a transcript of a NetNostalgia forum thread in which several adults from the Ohio River Valley share half-remembered fragments of a low-budget puppet show called Candle Cove that aired on a local UHF station (Channel 58) in the 1970s. The recollections grow progressively more disturbing — culminating in a 'Skin-Taker' marionette and an episode in which the puppets simply scream — before one user's mother delivers the closing twist: the television was tuned to static during those broadcasts. Candle Cove is widely cited as a foundational example of the creepypasta genre and was adapted as the first season of Syfy's anthology series Channel Zero in 2016. The work is a documented piece of fiction; Wyrdness catalogues it as an internet legend rather than a paranormal phenomenon.
origin: An internet phenomenon distributed through the Ichor Falls site, creepypasta wikis, Reddit, YouTube readings, and the Channel Zero television adaptation. The fictional setting is a UHF children's television program in the Huntington–Ashland (West Virginia / Kentucky / Ohio) media market.

etymology.origin: Coined by Kris Straub for the 2009 Ichor Falls story.
etymology.meaning: The fictional name of the in-universe children's television show.

timeline.event: Kris Straub publishes 'Candle Cove' on Ichor Falls
Syfy announces 'Channel Zero', an anthology series whose first season is based on Candle Cove
'Channel Zero: Candle Cove' premieres on Syfy
timeline.significance: Brings the creepypasta to a mainstream television audience

cultural_notes: Candle Cove is widely understood by readers to be fiction; the 'belief' aspect is in-genre roleplay rather than sincere claim.
